response.title: Can a power station keep my motorhome's full-size fridge and a CPAP going overnight, then recharge from the engine while I drive?
response.answer:
Yes. A portable power station can run your motorhome's full-size refrigerator and CPAP overnight, then recharge from your motorhome's engine while you're driving.

The key is choosing a power station with enough battery capacity, sufficient inverter power, and a dedicated alternator charging solution.

For a typical motorhome with a residential refrigerator (rather than an RV propane refrigerator), I'd start by looking at:

Battery capacity

3–4 kWh
Good starting range for overnight use

AC inverter

2,000 W+
With adequate compressor startup surge capacity

Engine charging

500–1,000 W
Using a compatible alternator charger

Target runtime

8–12 hrs
Depends on actual refrigerator consumption
1. How much electricity will you need overnight?

Here's an illustrative 10-hour estimate for a full-size residential refrigerator and a CPAP machine.

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed appliance ratings. Refrigerator consumption varies significantly with size, temperature, ambient heat, and compressor duty cycle.

After accounting for inverter losses and reserve capacity, a 3 kWh station could be sufficient for many setups, while 4 kWh gives you more flexibility.

2. Can driving recharge the battery before the next night?

Yes. Dedicated alternator chargers make this practical.

4. What I'd check before buying

Your refrigerator may already run through the RV's house-battery inverter, so connecting a portable power station requires planning. Avoid connecting its AC output to the RV's shore-power inlet without a properly designed transfer arrangement, since this can create unsafe backfeeding or charging loops.

## 1. How much electricity will you need overnight?

Here's an illustrative 10-hour estimate for a full-size residential refrigerator and a CPAP machine.

| Appliance | Estimated consumption |
|---|---:|
| Full-size residential refrigerator | 800–1,500 Wh |
| CPAP without heated humidifier | 100–250 Wh |
| CPAP with heated humidifier | 300–700 Wh |
| **Total overnight** | **900–2,200 Wh** |

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed appliance ratings. Refrigerator consumption varies significantly with size, temperature, ambient heat, and compressor duty cycle.

After accounting for inverter losses and reserve capacity, a 3 kWh station could be sufficient for many setups, while 4 kWh gives you more flexibility.

## 2. Can driving recharge the battery before the next night?

Yes. Dedicated alternator chargers make this practical.

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="center" gap={1}>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" flex="1" gap={1}>
      <icon name="truck" size="lg"/>
      <text weight="medium" size="xs">Engine / alternator</text>
    </box>
    <icon name="arrow-right" color="tertiary"/>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" flex="1" gap={1}>
      <icon name="zap" size="lg"/>
      <text weight="medium" size="xs">DC-DC charger</text>
    </box>
    <icon name="arrow-right" color="tertiary"/>
    <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" flex="1" gap={1}>
      <icon name="battery-charging" size="lg"/>
      <text weight="medium" size="xs">Power station</text>
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

For example, EcoFlow offers an 800W alternator charger, while Jackery offers a 600W DC-DC alternator charger. <Cite refs={["turn931901search0","turn931901search7"]}/>

Assuming 85% effective charging efficiency and enough spare alternator capacity:

| Driving time | 600W charger | 800W charger |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2 hours | 1.0 kWh | 1.4 kWh |
| 3 hours | 1.5 kWh | 2.0 kWh |
| 4 hours | 2.0 kWh | 2.7 kWh |
| 5 hours | 2.6 kWh | 3.4 kWh |

These are illustrative charging amounts, not guaranteed results. Power used by the refrigerator and other devices while driving reduces the net battery recharge.

**Important:** Have an RV electrical technician verify your alternator's spare capacity, cable sizing, fusing, and battery isolation. An 800W charger can draw substantial current from a 12V electrical system.

## 3. Calculate your battery requirements

{@body const [fridge,setFridge] = DIL.useState(110)}
{@body const [cpap,setCpap] = DIL.useState("50")}
{@body const [hours,setHours] = DIL.useState(10)}
{@body const [drive,setDrive] = DIL.useState(4)}
{@body const [charger,setCharger] = DIL.useState("800")}
{@body const energy = (fridge+Number(cpap))*hours}
{@body const capacity = Math.ceil(energy/0.75/100)*100}
{@body const recharge = Number(charger)*drive*0.85}

    <row justify="between" align="center">

      <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{fridge} W</text>

    </radio-group>

  </box>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <grid columns={2} gap={3}>
    <grid-item>
      <caption>Overnight appliance energy</caption>
      <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{(energy/1000).toFixed(2)} kWh</title>
    </grid-item>
    <grid-item>
      <caption>Suggested battery capacity</caption>
      <title size="xl" color="default" tabularNums>{(capacity/1000).toFixed(1)} kWh</title>
    </grid-item>
  </grid>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <box gap={1}>
    **Alternator charger**
    <segmented-control block size="md" value={charger} onChange={setCharger} options={[{"label":"600 W","value":"600"},{"label":"800 W","value":"800"},{"label":"1,000 W","value":"1000"}]}/>
  </box>
  <box gap={1}>
    <row justify="between" align="center">
      **Driving time**
      <text weight="medium" tabularNums>{drive} hours</text>
    </row>
    <slider min={1} max={8} step={0.5} value={drive} onChange={setDrive}/>
  </box>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} gap={2}>
    <row align="center" justify="between">
      <text weight="medium">Estimated energy added</text>
      **{(recharge/1000).toFixed(2)} kWh**
    </row>
    <box background="border" height="10px" radius="full" clip>
      <box background={recharge>=energy?"success-solid":"#D49A36"} height="100%" width={`${Math.min(100,recharge/energy*100)}%`} radius="full"/>

## 4. What I'd check before buying

Your refrigerator may already run through the RV's house-battery inverter, so connecting a portable power station requires planning. Avoid connecting its AC output to the RV's shore-power inlet without a properly designed transfer arrangement, since this can create unsafe backfeeding or charging loops.

For the CPAP, consider an approved DC power adapter to reduce inverter losses. Since it's essential overnight equipment, maintain a backup power option and test the entire setup before relying on it.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <form gap={3} onSubmit={()=>GenUI.issueNewTurn("My motorhome has a "+(fridgeType==="residential"?"120V residential refrigerator":fridgeType==="rv"?"RV propane/electric refrigerator":"refrigerator of unknown type")+". CPAP heated humidifier: "+cpapHeat+". Typical driving: "+dailyDrive+" per day. Recommend a suitably sized power station, alternator charger, and practical wiring arrangement.")}>

        <radio value="unknown">Not sure</radio>

      </radio-group>

        <radio value="6+ hours">6+ hours</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <button block submit>Find the right power setup <icon name="arrow-right" inline/></button>
  </form>
</box>

With those details, I can narrow down whether a 2, 3, or 4 kWh station makes sense and how quickly your motorhome can realistically recharge it.

text:
Yes. A portable power station can run your motorhome's full-size refrigerator and CPAP overnight, then recharge from your motorhome's engine while you're driving.

The key is choosing a power station with enough battery capacity, sufficient inverter power, and a dedicated alternator charging solution.

For a typical motorhome with a residential refrigerator (rather than an RV propane refrigerator), I'd start by looking at:

Battery capacity

3–4 kWh
Good starting range for overnight use

AC inverter

2,000 W+
With adequate compressor startup surge capacity

Engine charging

500–1,000 W
Using a compatible alternator charger

Target runtime

8–12 hrs
Depends on actual refrigerator consumption
1. How much electricity will you need overnight?

Here's an illustrative 10-hour estimate for a full-size residential refrigerator and a CPAP machine.

Appliance

	

Estimated consumption




Full-size residential refrigerator

	

800–1,500 Wh




CPAP without heated humidifier

	

100–250 Wh




CPAP with heated humidifier

	

300–700 Wh




Total overnight

	

900–2,200 Wh

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed appliance ratings. Refrigerator consumption varies significantly with size, temperature, ambient heat, and compressor duty cycle.

After accounting for inverter losses and reserve capacity, a 3 kWh station could be sufficient for many setups, while 4 kWh gives you more flexibility.

2. Can driving recharge the battery before the next night?

Yes. Dedicated alternator chargers make this practical.

Important: Have an RV electrical technician verify your alternator's spare capacity, cable sizing, fusing, and battery isolation. An 800W charger can draw substantial current from a 12V electrical system.

4. What I'd check before buying

Your refrigerator may already run through the RV's house-battery inverter, so connecting a portable power station requires planning. Avoid connecting its AC output to the RV's shore-power inlet without a properly designed transfer arrangement, since this can create unsafe backfeeding or charging loops.

For the CPAP, consider an approved DC power adapter to reduce inverter losses. Since it's essential overnight equipment, maintain a backup power option and test the entire setup before relying on it.

With those details, I can narrow down whether a 2, 3, or 4 kWh station makes sense and how quickly your motorhome can realistically recharge it.
